{{Short description|Conformal mapping in complex analysis}}
In [[complex analysis]], a '''Schwarz–Christoffel mapping''' is a [[conformal map]] of the [[upper half-plane]] or the complex [[unit disk]] onto the interior of a [[simple polygon]]. Such a map is [[existence theorem|guaranteed to exist]] by the [[Riemann mapping theorem]] (stated by [[Bernhard Riemann]] in 1851); the Schwarz–Christoffel formula provides an explicit construction. They were introduced independently by [[Elwin Bruno Christoffel|Elwin Christoffel]] in 1867<ref>{{Cite journal|title=Sul problema delle temperature stazionarie e la rappresentazione di una data superficie|url=http://link.springer.com/10.1007/BF02419161|journal=Annali di Matematica Pura ed Applicata|date=December 1867|issn=0373-3114|pages=89–103|volume=1|issue=1|doi=10.1007/BF02419161|language=it|first=Elwin Bruno|last=Christoffel|author-link=Elwin Bruno Christoffel}}</ref> and [[Hermann Amandus Schwarz|Hermann Schwarz]] in 1869.<ref>{{Cite journal|title=Ueber einige Abbildungsaufgaben.|url=https://www.degruyter.com/document/doi/10.1515/crll.1869.70.105/html|journal=Journal für die reine und angewandte Mathematik (Crelles Journal)|date=1869-01-01|issn=0075-4102|pages=105–120|volume=1869|issue=70|doi=10.1515/crll.1869.70.105|last=Schwarz|first=Hermann|author-link=Hermann Schwarz|url-access=subscription}}</ref>

Schwarz–Christoffel mappings are used in [[potential theory]] and some of its applications, including [[minimal surface]]s, [[Poincare disc model#Artistic realizations|hyperbolic art]], and [[fluid dynamics]].

== Definition ==
Consider a polygon in the complex plane. The [[Riemann mapping theorem]] implies that there is a [[biholomorphic]] mapping ''f'' from the upper half-plane
:<math> \{ \zeta \in \mathbb{C}: \operatorname{Im} \zeta > 0 \} </math>
to the  interior of the polygon.  The function ''f'' maps the real axis to the edges of the polygon. If the polygon has interior [[angle]]s <math>\alpha,\beta,\gamma, \ldots</math>, then this mapping is given by 
:<math>
f(\zeta) = \int^\zeta \frac{K}{(w-a)^{1-(\alpha/\pi)}(w-b)^{1-(\beta/\pi)}(w-c)^{1-(\gamma/\pi)} \cdots} \,\mathrm{d}w 
</math>
where <math>K</math> is a [[Constant (mathematics)|constant]], and <math>a < b < c < \cdots</math> are the values, along the real axis of the <math>\zeta</math> plane, of points corresponding to the vertices of the polygon in the <math>z</math> plane. A transformation of this form is called a ''Schwarz–Christoffel mapping''.

The integral can be simplified by mapping the [[point at infinity]] of the <math>\zeta</math> plane to one of the vertices of the <math>z</math> plane polygon. By doing this, the first factor in the formula becomes constant and so can be absorbed into the constant <math>K</math>. Conventionally, the point at infinity would be mapped to the vertex with angle <math>\alpha</math>.

In practice, to find a mapping to a specific polygon one needs to find the <math>a < b < c < \cdots</math> values which generate the correct polygon side lengths. This requires solving a set of nonlinear equations, and in most cases can only be done [[Numerical analysis|numerically]].<ref>{{Cite web|last=Driscoll|first=Toby|title=Schwarz-Christoffel mapping|url=http://www.math.udel.edu/~driscoll/research/conformal.html|access-date=2021-05-17|website=www.math.udel.edu}}</ref>

==Example==

Consider a semi-infinite strip in the {{math|<VAR >z</VAR >}} [[complex plane|plane]].  This may be regarded as a limiting form of a [[triangle]] with vertices {{math|<VAR >P</VAR > {{=}} 0}}, {{math|<VAR >Q</VAR > {{=}} &pi; ''i''}}, and {{math|<VAR >R</VAR >}} (with {{math|<VAR >R</VAR >}} real), as {{math|<VAR >R</VAR >}} tends to infinity.  Now {{math|&alpha; {{=}} 0}} and {{math|&beta; {{=}} &gamma; {{=}} {{frac|&pi;|2}}}} in the limit. Suppose we are looking for the mapping {{math|<VAR >f</VAR >}} with {{math|<VAR >f</VAR >(&minus;1) {{=}} <VAR >Q</VAR >}}, {{math|<VAR >f</VAR >(1) {{=}} <VAR >P</VAR >}}, and {{math|<VAR >f</VAR >(∞) {{=}} <VAR >R</VAR >}}. Then {{math|<VAR >f</VAR >}} is given by

:<math> f(\zeta) = \int^\zeta 
  \frac{K}{(w-1)^{1/2}(w+1)^{1/2}} \,\mathrm{d}w. \, </math>

Evaluation of this integral yields

: <math> z = f(\zeta) = C + K \operatorname{arcosh} \zeta, </math> <!-- NOTE: "arcosh" with one "c", not "arccosh" with two, since it corresponds to an area rather than to an arc. -->
<!-- :{{math|''z'' {{=}} ''f''(''&zeta;'') {{=}} ''C'' + ''K'' arccosh ''&zeta;''}} -->

where {{math|<VAR >C</VAR >}} is a (complex) constant of integration.  Requiring that {{math|<VAR >f</VAR >(&minus;1) {{=}} <VAR >Q</VAR >}} and {{math|<VAR >f</VAR >(1) {{=}} <VAR >P</VAR >}} gives {{math|<VAR >C</VAR > {{=}} 0}} and {{math|<VAR >K</VAR > {{=}} 1}}. Hence the Schwarz–Christoffel mapping is given by

:<math> z = \operatorname{arcosh} \zeta. </math> <!-- NOTE: "arcosh" with one "c", not "arccosh" with two, since it corresponds to an area rather than to an arc. -->
<!-- :{{math|''z'' {{=}} arccosh ''&zeta;''}} -->

This transformation is sketched below.

==Other simple mappings==

===Triangle===
A mapping to a plane [[triangle]] with interior angles <math>\pi a,\, \pi b</math> and <math>\pi(1-a-b)</math> is given by

:<math>z=f(\zeta)=\int^\zeta \frac{dw}{(w-1)^{1-a} (w+1)^{1-b}},</math>

which can be expressed in terms of [[hypergeometric function]]s or incomplete [[beta function]]s.

The upper half-plane is mapped to a triangle with circular arcs for edges by the [[Schwarz triangle map]].

===Square===
The upper half-plane is mapped to the square by

:<math>z=f(\zeta) = \int^\zeta \frac {\mathrm{d}w}{\sqrt{w(1-w^2)}}
=\sqrt{2} \, F\left(\sqrt{\zeta+1};\sqrt{2}/2\right),
</math>

where ''F'' is the incomplete [[elliptic integral]] of the first kind.

==See also==
* The [[Schwarzian derivative]] appears in the theory of Schwarz–Christoffel mappings.
